newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - RTZ-CRA's first-half profits slide 22 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - RTZ-CRA's first-half profits slide 22 pct.

text.p: Anglo-Australian mining giant RTZ-CRA reported a 22 percent slide in first-half 1996 earnings on Thursday, blaming lower industrial metal prices and other operational difficulties for the losses.
But the group remained upbeat for metals demand and prices over the rest of this year and into 1997.
"It's disappointing for us to have to report a drop in earnings," said Robert Wilson, chief executive of the group which merged in December last year.
"But in the longer term we are very optimistic about the future demand prospects (for metals)," he added.

Non-ferrous metal values dropped 11 percent overall during the first six months of the year, helping to drag net adjusted earnings before exceptional items down to $552 million from $711 million in the same period last year.
"Of that $159 (million) negative more than 100 percent can be accounted for by the fall in (metal) prices," Wilson said.
Metal prices hit earnings by $194 million and exchange rate changes by $34 million.

The main impact was from copper, the group's most important product. Prices averaged 115 cents a pound during the first half of 1996, down 13 percent from year-ago levels. The market has slumped to below 90 cents since. Wilson did not rule out further losses, saying another 20 percent drop in the red metal's value was possible but unlikely.
Every 10-cent fall in the price of copper hits net earnings by $90 million, according to RTZ-CRA's own estimates.

As well as falling prices, the first-half performance was hampered by a 28 percent drop in refined copper production, mainly because of delays in the production build-up at the firm's U.S. Kennecott smelter.
But unrefined output rose 17 percent to 363,000 tonnes as the group benefited from sharp increases from its 30 percent share in the huge Escondida mine in Chile.
Also depressing profits were operational problems and industrial relations disputes at RTZ-CRA's Australian coal mines, Wilson said.
On a more positive note group chairman Sir Derek Birkin said the price of many metals appeared to be lower than underlying fundamentals would suggest.
He was also upbeat about demand growth prospects.

"On a longer-term view, we are confident about growth of demand, especially from the Asian region which now accounts for a significant share of global consumption of all metals and minerals," he said.
Economic growth in Japan in Europe would start to accelerate while in the U.S. it may tail off, Wilson said separately.
Wilson said exploration at major new developments was showing good progress, particularly at the Grasberg copper/gold mine in Irian Jaya and diamond sites in Canada's North West Territories.

He added that the large number of projects under development meant RTZ-CRA's annual capital expenditure would probably rise beyind the current $1.5 billion. But this should not stretch the company's balance sheet unduly.
"If capital expenditure rises hugely it would have significant financial implications. We are a long way from that," Wilson said.
The reaction to the results on the London stock exchange was positive. Shares rose as much as 35-1/2p to 966p early on Thursday before edging back to 960p by 1130 GMT.
Analysts pointed to a future recovery in metal prices.
"Sir Derek Birkin's statement talks about metal prices being more depressed than fundamentals would indicate," said Charles Kernot, mining analyst at Paribas Capital Markets.
"That could mean things could move higher over the next couple of years as prices go up with economic growth."
